q: An opponent complains that a racket covering is too glossy. With no glossometer available, what practical test does the HMO suggest?
options: Hold a plastic net gauge at an angle to the surface: if its letters can be clearly read in the reflection, it is too glossy
Rub the surface with a towel and see whether it squeaks
Compare it with the umpire's own racket
Shine a torch on it and measure the glare
detail: Glossiness can be measured with an EEL glossometer, but this is rarely available. As a guide, a covering is **too glossy if letters can be clearly distinguished** when, say, a **plastic net gauge** is placed at an angle to the surface. The umpire only checks this **if the opponent complains**.

q: Which markings must be clearly visible near the handle on an ITTF-authorised racket covering? Select all that apply.
options: The ITTF logo
The supplier's logo or trademark
The ITTF number, when present
The player's name
The covering's thickness in mm
detail: Authorised coverings carry the **ITTF logo**, the **ITTF number (when present)** and the **supplier's logo or trademark**, attached so they are clearly visible near the handle. The markings alone **do not prove** the covering is currently authorised: check it against the current list (LARC).

q: A covering carries the ITTF logo. Is that enough to accept it?
options: No: check it against the current List of Authorised Racket Coverings (LARC), and check its thickness
Yes: the ITTF logo proves it is authorised
Yes, if the supplier's logo is also present
Only the referee may check coverings
detail: The ITTF marking is required but **is not proof** that the covering is currently authorised. The umpire checks it against the **current LARC**. Even an authorised covering may be illegal, for example if a thicker sponge was fitted or gluing made it swell.

q: A player's racket fails the pre-match test at the racket control centre. There is no time to test a replacement before the match. What happens?
options: The racket is confiscated; the player uses another racket, which is tested after the match
The player may use the failed racket and is tested again after the match
The match is delayed until a replacement has been tested
The player is disqualified
detail: A racket that fails a pre-match test is **confiscated** and the player must use a different racket. If there is no time to test the replacement first, **it is tested after the match**. A racket that passes is marked and handed to the umpire in a paper envelope.

q: Between games you notice a player is now using a different racket, although the first one was not damaged. What do you do?
options: Suspend play immediately and report to the referee, who may disqualify the player
Inspect the new racket, show it to the opponent and continue
Award a penalty point to the opponent
Give the player a yellow card
detail: A player may not change racket during a match **unless it is accidentally damaged so badly that it cannot be used**. If you find an undamaged racket has been changed, **suspend play immediately and report to the referee**, who **may disqualify** the player.

q: With your agreement, a player takes their racket off the table during the interval between games. What must happen before the next game?
options: You and the opponent must be given the chance to inspect the racket (or its replacement)
Nothing: you agreed to its removal
The racket must be re-tested at racket control
The player loses the next point
detail: Rackets must stay on the table during intervals unless the umpire agrees otherwise. If one is removed, **the umpire and the opponent must be able to inspect it, or its replacement, before the next game**. The only exception is a Para player whose racket is strapped to the hand.

q: A racket becomes damaged mid-match and the player wants to carry on with it. You doubt it is still legal. What happens?
options: Report to the referee, who decides mainly on the interests of the opponent
Decide yourself; the player's wishes come first
Allow it: a racket legal at the start stays legal
Order an immediate replacement
detail: If the umpire has any doubt about a damaged racket's legality, **report immediately to the referee**. The referee should consider **primarily the interests of the opponent**, since the ball may rebound unpredictably. Unless the damage is trivial, replacing the racket is generally better.

q: Where may players use liquid glue to attach coverings at an ITTF event?
options: Only in the ventilated gluing area provided by the organisers, and only glues without harmful solvents
Anywhere in the playing hall, if the glue is ITTF approved
In the changing rooms only
At the table, during the practice period
detail: Coverings may be attached only with pressure-sensitive adhesive sheets or **liquid adhesives without harmful solvents**. Organisers provide a **properly ventilated gluing area**, and liquid glues must not be used anywhere else in the hall, including changing rooms and practice and spectator areas.

q: Why does it matter exactly when the ball is “in play”?
options: Only while the ball is in play can a point (other than a penalty point) be scored
It decides when the timer for expedite starts
It decides when advice may be given
It only matters in doubles
detail: It is essential to know when the ball is in play, because **only during this time can a point, other than a penalty point, be scored**.

q: After playing a stroke, a player's racket slips out of their hand and hits the net post. The ball is still in play. What is your decision?
options: Point to the opponent
Let: it was an accident
Play on: the racket was no longer held
Point to the opponent only if the net moved
detail: The racket was being carried at the start of the rally, so it counts as **anything the player wears or carries**. If it **touches the net assembly** while the ball is in play, the opponent scores. The net post is part of the net assembly.

q: A's return crosses the net, then flies outwards over B's side line without touching B's court. B catches it beside the table. What is your decision?
options: Point to B: there is no obstruction when the ball has passed outward over the side line
Point to A: obstruction
Let
Point to A: B touched the ball in play
detail: There is no obstruction if the interception happens when the ball **has passed outward over the side line**, beyond the end line, or is otherwise moving away from the playing surface. A's return missed, so **B scores**.

q: The ball hits a player's racket-hand forearm, above the wrist, and goes over onto the opponent's court. What is your decision?
options: Point to the opponent: it was not struck
Good return: it is the racket arm
Let
Good return if the racket also touched it
detail: A player strikes the ball only with the **racket held in the hand** or the **racket hand below the wrist**. The forearm above the wrist does not count, so the return is not good.

q: The server tosses correctly from behind the end line, but leans in and strikes the ball when it is above the playing surface, inside the end line. What is your decision?
options: Fault: the ball must be behind the end line until struck
Legal: the toss started behind the end line
Let, and warn the server
Legal, as the ball was above the playing surface

diagram.alt: Side view: the ball is struck above the table, inside the server's end line

detail: From the start of service **until it is struck**, the ball must be above the level of the playing surface **and behind the server's end line**. Signal and verbal explanation: **“inside the end line”**.

umpire.signal: Point signal to the receiver, then the “inside the end line” signal

q: Two services are thrown from and struck at the same place. One toss is low, the other high. Why might only the low one be a fault?
options: The lower the toss, the more a sideways movement shows it was not near vertical
Low tosses are always faults
High tosses are always legal
Only the height matters, never the angle
detail: The **height of the toss is a factor** in deciding whether it is near vertical. If the ball travels the same sideways distance, a **low toss** rises at a clearly diagonal angle, while a **high toss** stays within a few degrees of vertical.

q: You are umpiring alone. A player serves so close to the end line and their body that you cannot be sure the service is legal. Whose responsibility is that?
options: The player's: they must serve so the umpire can be satisfied the service is legal
The umpire's: give the benefit of the doubt every time
The referee's: call them to watch
Nobody's: services that can't be judged are always legal
detail: It is **the player's responsibility to serve so that the umpire or AU can be satisfied** the service complies, and either may decide a service is incorrect. A player who serves near the margins of illegality **runs the risk of being penalised**.

q: A player's service action is only just acceptable. Without a formal warning, may the umpire say anything?
options: Yes: they may tell the player informally, between rallies, that any deterioration could make it illegal
No: any comment counts as the formal warning
No: the umpire must stay silent
Only the referee may speak to players about services
detail: Whether or not a formal warning is given, a player whose action is **only marginally acceptable** may be **advised informally, between rallies**, by the umpire or AU, that any deterioration could make it illegal.

q: First occasion in the match: the assistant umpire is unsure whether a service was legal. What does the AU do?
options: Raise an arm, call “Stop”, warn the server and advise the umpire, who calls “Let”
Call “Fault” and advise the umpire
Do nothing: only the umpire may warn
Show a yellow card to the server
detail: Either official may give the single service warning. When the AU decides, the AU **raises an arm above the head, calls “Stop”, warns the server and advises the umpire**, who calls **“Let”** and repeats the score.

au.call: “Stop”, warn the server, advise the umpire

q: The server was warned earlier. Now the assistant umpire judges another service to be of doubtful legality. What happens?
options: The AU raises an arm and calls “Fault”; the umpire signals the point to the receiver and calls the new score
The AU warns the server again
The umpire decides whether to accept the AU's call
Let, because only the umpire can award the point
detail: After the warning, a doubtful service is a fault. The AU **raises an arm above the head**, calls **“Fault”** and, if necessary, advises the umpire, who **indicates the point for the receiver** and calls the new score. The umpire may not overrule the AU on service legality.

q: Doubles. The server's partner stands so that, at the moment of contact, the receiver cannot see the ball. What is your decision?
options: Fault: the ball must not be hidden by the server's partner
Let: ask the partner to move
Legal: only the server's own body counts
Legal if the umpire could see the ball
detail: The ball must not be hidden from the receiver **by the server or their doubles partner**, or by anything they wear or carry. If asked, use the “hidden” signal and say **“hidden by partner”**.

umpire.signal: Point signal to the receivers, then the “hidden” signal

q: The server starts with the ball resting on the fingertips rather than the palm. If asked, what is the standard verbal explanation?
options: “Ball resting on the fingers”
“Palm not open”
“Not vertically”
“Hidden”
detail: The illegal-service signals have matching short explanations: **“Not high enough”**, **“Palm not open”**, **“Ball resting on the fingers”**, **“Below the playing surface”**, **“Inside the end line”**, **“Not vertically”** and **“Hidden by …”**.

q: A player cannot straighten the fingers of the free hand because of a disability recorded on their classification card. How may they serve?
options: From a curved palm: the umpire relaxes the requirement
They must still use an open, flat palm
They must serve with the racket hand
Only after the referee approves each service
detail: The umpire may relax service requirements where a physical disability prevents compliance. The International Classification Card lists such limitations, so a player may, for example, **serve from a curved palm** or **toss from a stump**.

q: The server flicks the ball off the fingers so it spins visibly as it rises 20 cm. What is your decision?
options: Fault: the ball must be projected without spin
Legal: it rose more than 16 cm
Let, and warn the server
Legal: spin only matters after the strike
detail: The ball must be projected **near vertically upwards, without imparting spin**. The open-palm rule exists so the server cannot grip and spin the ball.

q: A ball arrives from outside and above the level of the playing surface and clips the edge. What best indicates it touched the playing surface rather than the side?
options: It travels upwards after contact
It continues downwards after contact
It makes a loud sound
The receiver could not return it
detail: There is no infallible guide, but if after touching the edge **the ball travels upwards**, it probably touched the playing surface. If it **continues downwards**, it more likely touched the side.

q: The ball hits the edge of the table while still rising from below the level of the playing surface. What is the most likely decision?
options: Side: it almost certainly touched the side, so the return is not good
Edge: the return is good
Let
Edge, if it bounced upwards
detail: If the ball first passed over the playing surface, the return is good. If it touched the table **while still rising from below the level of the playing surface**, it **almost certainly touched the side**.

q: You (the umpire) clearly see a player move the playing surface. A moment later the ball clips the table on the AU's side and the AU calls “Side”. What is the decision?
options: Your earlier decision stands: point to the opponent of the player who moved the table
The AU's “Side” call decides the point
Let, because the calls conflict
Ask the referee
detail: One official's decision may be **pre-empted** by an earlier decision of the other. Whether the ball touched the edge on the AU's side is **irrelevant if the umpire has already seen a player move the playing surface**.

q: You declare a let because a ball from another table rolls into the court. At the same moment the AU judges the service illegal. What is the decision?
options: Let: your decision came first, so the service is not penalised
Point to the receiver: the AU's service decision stands
Replay the point and warn the server
Ask the referee
detail: Service legality is normally the AU's decision to make, but it can be **pre-empted**: a service the AU judges illegal **may not be penalised if the umpire has already declared a let**, for example because a ball from another table came into the playing area.

q: A player repeatedly uses an unsporting tactic that is not against any law. May the umpire award a point to the opponent?
options: No: points may only be awarded for reasons supported by the laws
Yes: the umpire may award points for unfair actions
Yes, after a warning
Only in team matches
detail: The umpire must **never award points for reasons not supported by the laws**, for example because a player “deserves” it or another acted unfairly. Every decision must be justifiable by reference to a law. Misbehaviour is dealt with through the behaviour regulations.

q: A player's free hand brushes the playing surface mid-rally, but play continues. What should the umpire do?
options: Stop play: raise an arm, call “Stop”, then give the new score and explanation
Let the rally finish, then award the point to whoever wins it
Let the rally finish, then award the point to the opponent
Declare a let
detail: Some infringements **do not automatically stop play**, so the umpire must stop it: **raise an arm above the head, call “Stop”**, then call the new score and, if not obvious, the explanation (here “hand on table”).

umpire.signal: Raise arm above head, then the point signal

q: Both players are sure your decision on the last rally was wrong, and you accept you may have been mistaken. What should you do?
options: Accept the correction
Keep your decision: umpires never change decisions
Declare a let
Ask the referee to decide
detail: Exceptionally, where **both players or pairs are sure a decision is wrong** and the umpire can accept they may have been mistaken, the umpire **would be wise to accept the correction**. A request from only the player who would benefit is not enough.

q: After the next rally has started, a player asks you to reconsider a decision from the previous rally. What do you do?
options: Ignore the request
Stop play and reconsider it
Reconsider it at the end of the current rally
Refer it to the referee
detail: A request for reconsideration **should be ignored once another rally has started**.

q: During a rally, a loud bang from the stands startles both players. What do you do?
options: Declare a let
Play on: crowd noise is part of the game
Wait until the end of the rally, then decide
Award the point to whoever wins the rally, then warn the crowd
detail: A disturbance outside the players' control that may affect the outcome, such as **a sudden noise loud enough to startle the players**, justifies a let. It is better to declare it immediately than wait until the rally ends.

q: A player trips over a surround and loses the rally. The surround was in place at the start of the rally. When might a let still be given?
options: If the incident disturbs the conditions of play in a way that could disadvantage the opponent
Always, because the player tripped
If the player asks immediately
Never
detail: Hazards present at the start of a rally don't normally justify a let: the player who trips is **not entitled** to one. But a let **may be allowed if the incident disturbs the conditions of play in a way that could be disadvantageous to the opponent**, for example a surround falling into the opponent's area.

q: Doubles. A service touches the net, then lands in the receiver's left half-court. What is your decision?
options: Point to the receivers
Let: the ball touched the net
Let, and warn the server
Replay the service

diagram.alt: Top view, doubles: the service clips the net and lands in the receiver's left half-court

detail: A net service is only a let **if the service is otherwise correct**. In doubles it must land in the receiver's **right** half-court. Here it lands on the wrong half-court, so it is a fault and **the receivers score**.

q: A low return squeezes under the net (between the net and the playing surface) and lands on the opponent's court. What is your decision?
options: Point to the opponent of the striker
Good return
Let: the net must be adjusted
Good return if the net was too high
detail: A player scores if the ball, struck by the opponent, passes **through the net, between the net and the net post, or between the net and the playing surface**. This is why the bottom of the net must be as close as possible to the surface.

q: Doubles, last possible game. One pair reaches 5 points first. What happens? Select all that apply.
options: The players change ends
The pair due to receive next changes its order of receiving
Players may take a brief towelling break
The serving pair changes its order of serving
A 1-minute interval is taken
detail: In the last possible game, when one pair first scores 5, the **ends change** and **the pair due to receive next changes its order of receiving**. Towelling is permitted at this change of ends. There is no interval and the serving order stays the same.

q: Doubles, game 1. A served first to X. The score is 4-2 (6 points played). Who serves, and to whom?
options: Y serves to A
B serves to Y
X serves to B
A serves to X
detail: Service changes every 2 points and rotates A→X, X→B, B→Y, Y→A. After 6 points (three changes), **Y serves to A**.

q: Doubles. In game 1, A served first to X, so the order was A→X→B→Y. In game 2, X/Y choose Y to serve first. Who receives first?
options: B
A
X
The receiving pair chooses
detail: In later games the first receiver is **the player who served to the chosen server in the previous game**. In game 1, **B served to Y**, so B receives first.

q: Deciding game of a doubles match. At 5-2 the ends were changed, but the receiving pair forgot to change its order of receiving. You notice at 7-5. What do you do?
options: Stop play, correct the receiving order, and continue at 7‑5
Go back to 5‑2 and replay
Continue: the error is too late to correct
Correct the order and deduct points scored since 5‑2
detail: As soon as an order error is discovered, play stops and resumes with the **correct server and receiver at the score reached**. **All points scored before the discovery count.**

umpire.call: Correct the order, repeat the score “7-5”

q: In a doubles game, the pair that should have served first did not. You can't know which of them would have served first. What do you do?
options: Ask them immediately who would have been their first server, then work out the order
Decide by lot
The player who served most recently is deemed first server
Restart the game at 0‑0
detail: If the pair who should have served first did not, the umpire **cannot know which of them would have served first**, so should **ask them immediately** and then calculate the order in which play resumes.

q: What should the umpire record to be able to correct doubles order errors?
options: The striking order at the start of the match, and the first server in each game
Only the first server of the match
Every server at every change of service
Nothing: the AU keeps track
detail: The umpire should note **the striking order at the start of the match** and **the first server in each game**, so any error can be corrected from the right starting point. Between games, wait until both pairs are back before asking who will serve.

q: Singles, best of 5 games. A served first in game 1. Who serves first in game 5, and when do the players change ends?
options: A; when the first player reaches 5 points
B; when the first player reaches 5 points
A; at 6 points
B; there is no change of ends in game 5
detail: The first server alternates each game (A, B, A, B, **A**). Game 5 is the last possible game, so ends change **when the first player scores 5**.

q: Doubles, game 1. A served first to X (order A→X→B→Y). The score reaches 10-10. Who serves, and to whom?
options: B serves to Y
A serves to X
X serves to B
Y serves to A
detail: 20 points means 10 changes of service. The rotation has 4 steps, so 10 changes lands on the third step: **B→Y**. From now on service changes after every point (Y→A next).

q: During the toss for serve and ends, where should the umpire make sure the coin or disc does not land?
options: On the table, and preferably not on the floor
Anywhere is fine
Only not on the floor
In the umpire's hand
detail: Toss the two-coloured disc or coin in front of both players, making sure they know how to call. **Do not let it fall onto the table and, preferably, not onto the floor.**

q: In a doubles match between A/B and X/Y, how many different striking orders are possible?
detail: Only **two** orders are possible: **A-X-B-Y** and **A-Y-B-X**, though the sequence may start with any player.

q: An error in the serving order is discovered. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Play is interrupted as soon as the error is discovered
Play resumes with the correct server and receiver at the score reached
All points scored before the discovery count
In doubles, the order follows the choice made by the pair serving first in that game
Points scored while the error persisted are replayed
The game restarts at 0‑0
detail: Play is interrupted **as soon as the error is discovered** and resumes with the correct players **at the score reached**, following the sequence set at the start of the match and, in doubles, the serving order chosen in that game. **All points scored before the discovery are reckoned.**

q: A match is the best of 7 games. How many games must a player win?
detail: A match is **the best of any odd number of games**. Best of 7 is won by the first to **4** games.

q: Under the expedite system, the receiver wins the point after how many correct returns in a rally?
detail: If the receiving player or pair makes **13 correct returns** in a rally, the receiver scores. The count includes the return of service.

q: The 10-minute limit is reached during a rally at 6-5 (11 points). Who serves next?
options: The player who served in the interrupted rally
The player who received in the interrupted rally
Whoever is due by the normal rotation
Decided by lot
detail: If **the ball is in play** when time is reached, the umpire interrupts play and it resumes with service by **the player who served in the interrupted rally**.

umpire.call: “Let”, announce that expedite applies, repeat the score

q: The 10-minute limit is reached between rallies, at 6-5 (11 points). Who serves next?
options: The player who received in the previous rally
The player who served in the previous rally
Whoever is due by the normal rotation
The player who is behind
detail: If **the ball is not in play** when expedite comes into operation, play resumes with service by **the player who received in the immediately preceding rally**.

q: How should the stroke counter count under the expedite system?
options: Aloud, “one” to “thirteen”, counting the receiver's returns including the return of service, right after each stroke
Silently, then announce the total at the end of the rally
Aloud, counting every stroke by both players
Aloud, but only after each return lands
detail: The stroke counter counts **aloud the receiver's return strokes, including the return of service, from “one” to “thirteen”**, calling **immediately after the receiver strikes the ball**, not after the return lands.

q: The receiver's 13th return is good. What does the umpire do?
options: Call “Stop” and award the point to the receiver
Let the rally continue until someone misses
Declare a let
Award the point to the server
detail: If the 13th return is good, **the umpire calls “stop” and awards the point to the receiver**.

q: Singles. Expedite came in during game 2, which B finished serving. A served first in game 1. Who serves first in game 3?
options: A: expedite does not change the order set at the start of the match
B, who served last in game 2
A's opponent, because of expedite
Decided by lot
detail: Introducing expedite **does not alter the order of serving and receiving in the match**. At the start of each game the first server is determined by the original order (A in games 1, 3, 5…), even if the same player served at the end of the previous game.

q: For the 10-minute expedite limit, when should the timekeeper stop the clock? Select all that apply.
options: During towelling breaks
At the change of ends in the last possible game
While the ball is retrieved from outside the playing area
During appeals to the referee
While the ball is retrieved within the playing area
Between every rally
detail: The timer is stopped during **significant breaks**: towelling, the change of ends in the last possible game, retrieving the ball from **outside** the playing area, and appeals to the referee. Retrieving it **within** the playing area is not a reason to stop the timer.

q: The 10-minute limit is reached at 9-8. Is the expedite system introduced?
options: Yes: only 17 points have been scored
No: at least 18 points have been scored
Only if both players agree
Only from the next game
detail: Expedite is not introduced if **at least 18 points** have been scored. 9 + 8 = **17**, so it is introduced.

q: The 10-minute limit is reached at 10-8. Is the expedite system introduced?
options: No: 18 points have been scored
Yes: the time limit has been reached
Yes, from 10‑10
Only if both players agree
detail: 10 + 8 = **18** points, so expedite **is not introduced** in this game. It may still be introduced in a later game when that game's time limit is reached (with fewer than 18 points).

q: The assistant umpire is the timekeeper. The 10-minute limit is reached. What happens?
options: The AU raises an arm and calls “Time”; the umpire declares a let if needed and announces expedite
The umpire waits for the end of the game
The AU tells the players directly
The stroke counter announces expedite
detail: The timekeeper calls **“Time”** loudly (the AU also raises an arm). The umpire then **declares a let if necessary** and tells the players that the rest of the match is played under the expedite system, repeating the score.

umpire.signal: Raise arm above head, after the AU's signal and call
umpire.call: “Let” if necessary, announce expedite, repeat the score

q: A player believes the referee's rule interpretation was wrong. What further appeal is possible?
options: Their Association can appeal to the ITTF Rules Committee, whose ruling applies to future cases but cannot change the referee's decision
The player can appeal to the jury, who can replay the match
None: the referee's word is final for ever
The umpire can overrule the referee
detail: The referee's decision is final on rule interpretation for that event. **The player's Association** may appeal to the **ITTF Rules Committee**, which gives a ruling **for future occasions** but **cannot change the referee's decision**.

q: In an individual event, a player appeals to the referee and their coach starts arguing the case. What should the referee do?
options: Deal only with the player; an interpreter may help with language
Let the coach present the appeal
Deal only with the coach
Ask the umpire to argue against the coach
detail: In an individual event the referee deals **only with the player or pair**. A coach or captain should not be allowed to intercede, but **an interpreter may assist** where there is a language difficulty.

q: In a team match, a player protests a decision but the team captain does not support the protest. What happens?
options: The protest is ignored
The referee hears it anyway
The umpire decides alone
It is recorded and heard after the match
detail: In a team match, **any protest by a player that is not supported by the team captain should be ignored**.

q: An appeal is made against the action of the assistant umpire. Who takes part in the discussion?
options: Only that official; others may give a statement if asked, then take no further part
All match officials
The umpire, the AU and both players' coaches
Anyone who saw the incident
detail: When the appeal is against a match official's action, **only that official** takes part in the argument. The referee may hear another official or a witness, but **once they have made a statement they take no further part**.

q: An umpire officiates alone, with no assistant umpire. What is the umpire responsible for? Select all that apply.
options: All edge-ball decisions
All aspects of service
All timings
Counting strokes under expedite, with no help
Rule interpretation disputes
detail: An umpire working alone has the final decision on all questions of fact, **including all edge balls and all aspects of service**, and is responsible **for all timings**. Under expedite, **another official acts as stroke counter**. Rule interpretation remains the referee's.

q: Where is the recommended position for the stroke counter?
options: Standing next to the umpire, so the umpire can clearly hear the count
Sitting at the referee's desk
Behind one end of the table
Next to the score indicator, sitting
detail: The recommended position is **standing next to the umpire**. If that blocks TV or spectators, stand next to the AU; exceptionally, sit next to the umpire.

q: How are the Laws of Table Tennis changed, compared with the Regulations for International Competitions?
options: Laws: at a General Meeting with a 75% majority. Regulations: by the ITTF Board, simple majority
Both by the Board, simple majority
Laws: by the Board. Regulations: by a General Meeting
Both at a General Meeting, 75% majority
detail: A **law** can be changed only at a **General Meeting** with **75%** of those voting. **Regulations** can be changed at a meeting of the **ITTF Board of Directors** by **simple majority**.

q: When is the umpire advised to stand, and should the assistant umpire ever stand?
options: Umpire: in doubles if the seat is too low to see the half-courts. AU: should not stand for doubles
Umpire: always in singles. AU: always in doubles
Both always stand in doubles
Neither ever stands
detail: For doubles, the umpire is advised to **stand if the seat isn't high enough** to see whether service bounces in the correct half-courts. Standing for singles isn't recommended. The **AU should not stand for doubles**.

q: Both players ask for a time-out at the same moment. What applies?
options: Up to 1 minute; play resumes earlier only if both are ready; neither gets another time-out
2 minutes, one for each player
Each may still take another time-out later
Only the first to signal gets a time-out
detail: If both request a time-out at the same time, the time allowed is still **up to 1 minute**, and they **need not return earlier unless both are ready**. **Neither is entitled to another time-out** in that match.

q: Player A takes a time-out. Before play resumes, player B also requests one. Is this allowed?
options: Yes
No: only one time-out per break
Only if A agrees
Only in team matches
detail: In the unlikely event of one player requesting a time-out and the other also requesting one **before play has resumed, this is allowed**.

q: A player already had a very short injury break. They now need brief treatment again. What may the referee allow?
options: Exceptionally, another brief interval, as long as the total suspension in the match does not exceed 10 minutes
Another full 10 minutes
Nothing: only one injury break per match, ever
Up to 5 more minutes, regardless of the first
detail: Normally only one recovery interval is allowed per match. **Exceptionally**, if the first was very short, another brief interval may be allowed if it doesn't prejudice the opponent and **the total suspension in the match does not exceed 10 minutes**.

q: A player is injured and the referee is called. When does the timekeeper start timing the suspension?
options: When the referee is called
When the referee arrives
When treatment starts
When the player leaves the table
detail: The timekeeper times the suspension **from the time the referee is called**, not from when they arrive at the playing area.

q: At 3-2 the ball is hit far outside the playing area. While it is fetched, a player towels down. Is this acceptable?
options: Yes: towelling is fine when it causes no further interruption
No: towelling is only allowed every 6 points
Only if the umpire gives a time-out
Only with the opponent's consent
detail: There is no reason why players may not towel **at times that don't further interrupt play**, such as **when the ball is being retrieved from outside the playing area**, as long as players don't cause such breaks deliberately.

q: When a time-out ends, what does the assistant umpire do with the signboard or white marker?
options: Removes it from the table and places a white marker by the score indicator, next to the requesting player's score
Leaves it on the table until the end of the game
Gives it to the referee
Places it on the opponent's court
detail: The signboard is removed from the table and **a white marker is placed near the score indicator, next to the score of the player or pair who took the time-out**, to show their time-out has been used.

q: Game 2, the score is 10-9 to B. Player A, already on 1 penalty point, misbehaves again, so B is awarded 2 penalty points. What happens?
options: B wins game 2 at 11‑9, and game 3 starts 1‑0 to B
B wins game 2 at 12‑9
B wins game 2 at 11‑9; the extra point is lost
The 2 points are both carried into game 3
detail: Penalty points can complete a game. **Unused points carry over** to the next game of that match, so it starts **0-1 (or 0-2) in favour of the offender's opponent**. If the match has ended, unused points are ignored.

q: Penalty points are awarded after the final point of the match. What happens to them?
options: They are ignored
They carry over to the player's next match
They change the match result
They are converted to a fine
detail: Unused penalty points are carried to the next game **if the match has not ended**. If the match has ended, **they are ignored**. The incident should still be recorded on the scoresheet.

q: A game starts at 0-1 because of a carried-over penalty point. Who serves first?
options: Whoever should be serving at that score by the sequence set at the start of the match
The offender's opponent
The offender
Decided by lot
detail: When a game starts at 0-1 or 0-2, **the server is the one who should be serving at that score** according to the sequence established at the start of the match.

q: In a team match, a player was formally warned in their first singles. They misbehave in their second singles. What happens?
options: The warning carries over, so they are penalised with a penalty point
A new yellow card warning, since it is a new match
Nothing until a second offence
They are disqualified
detail: In a team match, **warnings and penalties carry over to subsequent individual matches**. The first offence in the second match is treated as a repeat offence, so **1 penalty point** is awarded.

q: Team match. In earlier singles, A was warned and B incurred 1 penalty point. A and B now play doubles together, and A commits a first offence. What is the penalty?
options: 2 penalty points
1 penalty point
A yellow card warning
Disqualification
detail: A doubles pair takes **the higher of the warnings or penalties of either player**. B already had 1 penalty point, so the pair's next offence earns **2 penalty points**, whichever player commits it.

q: In a team match, what carries forward from one individual match to the next?
options: Cards (warnings and penalty status), but not the penalty points themselves
Penalty points, but not cards
Both cards and penalty points
Nothing
detail: **Cards carry forward between individual matches** (singles and doubles), **but penalty points do not**. A player's next match does not start with points awarded against them, but their disciplinary status continues.

q: A coach who has already been formally warned keeps protesting loudly. What do you do?
options: Show a red card, send the coach away, and report it to the referee
Award a penalty point against the player
Give a second yellow card
Ignore it: coaches can't be penalised
detail: Penalty points cannot be given against a coach, and it would be unfair to give them against the player. After a formal warning, a coach who continues misbehaving is **shown a red card and sent away** until the end of the match (or team match), and **the incident is reported to the referee**.

q: A player keeps misbehaving after receiving 2 penalty points. What follows?
options: The umpire suspends play and reports to the referee, who would normally disqualify the player
A third penalty of 3 points
The umpire disqualifies the player
Another yellow card
detail: After the warning, 1 point and 2 points, the umpire **suspends play and reports to the referee**. The referee would **normally disqualify** the player, showing a **red card**.

q: For serious misbehaviour, from what may the referee disqualify a player? Select all that apply.
options: The match
The event
The whole competition
All future ITTF events
detail: The referee may disqualify a player **from a match, an event or a whole competition**, depending on the gravity. In very serious cases they also report formally to the player's Association.

q: When is it appropriate to penalise the player, rather than the adviser, for illegal advice?
options: Only when it is clear the player is seeking the advice
Always: the player is responsible for their adviser
Never
When the adviser has already been sent away
detail: The penalty point system for illegal advice should be limited to situations where **it is clear the player is seeking advice**. It would be unfair to penalise a player for advice they didn't seek; usually deal directly with the adviser.

q: A doubles pair from two Associations has two nominated advisers. Adviser 1 was warned for illegal advice. Now adviser 2 advises during a rally. What do you do?
options: Send both advisers away: they are treated as a single unit
Warn adviser 2: it is their first offence
Send away adviser 2 only
Award a penalty point to the opponents
detail: Advisers of a mixed-Association pair are **treated as a single unit**. One warning applies to both, and if **either gives illegal advice after either has been warned, both are sent away**.

q: In a team match, you show a yellow card to one person on the team bench for illegal advice. Who does the warning apply to?
options: Everyone on that team bench
Only that person
Only the team captain
The player at the table
detail: In a team match, a warning for illegal advice **applies to everyone on the team bench**. If anyone on the bench advises illegally again, that person is shown a red card and sent away.

q: In a team event, an adviser who was sent away is also a player in the team. When may they return?
options: Only to play their own individual match, then leave again until the team match ends
After the current individual match
Not at all: the team plays without them
After 10 minutes
detail: In a team event a dismissed adviser may not return until the end of the team match, **except to play**, and then **only for the duration of their own individual match**.

q: After losing a point, a player angrily smashes the ball out of the playing area. Which standard umpire's call describes this?
options: Ball abuse
Equipment abuse
Unsportsmanlike conduct
Time-wasting
detail: **Ball abuse**: violently, dangerously or angrily hitting, kicking or throwing the ball, including intentionally or recklessly hitting it out of the playing area. Other calls include racket abuse, equipment abuse, verbal and physical abuse, audible and visible obscenity, time-wasting and unsportsmanlike conduct.

q: A shirt has a solid orange panel covering about 40% of the front. The ball is orange. Can the shirt be legal?
options: Possibly not: a solid patch of 40% can still be the dominant colour
Yes: less than half the shirt is orange
Yes: only the back of the shirt matters
Yes, if the referee hasn't banned it before
detail: The “main” colour doesn't necessarily mean the largest area. A **solid patch covering only 40% of the front can still be the dominant colour**, while more of the same colour evenly dispersed may be unnoticeable. What matters is **the apparent colour** and the ball's visibility.

q: At a World, Olympic or Paralympic title competition, what is the rule for players from the same Association?
options: They must be dressed uniformly, except possibly socks, shoes and advertisements
They may wear any legal clothing
They must wear identical socks and shoes too
Only doubles partners must match
detail: In World, Olympic or Paralympic title competitions, players of the same Association must be **dressed uniformly**, except possibly **socks, shoes** and the number, size, colour and design of **advertisements**. In other events doubles pairs may wear different colours.

q: A player wears cycling shorts under their shorts to keep their muscles warm. What is the recommendation?
options: Allowed; they should be the same colour as the shorts and carry no advertisements or markings
Not allowed
Allowed in any colour, with advertisements
Allowed only with a medical certificate
detail: Cycling shorts under shorts or a skirt are generally accepted. They **should be the same colour as the shorts or skirt** and **must not carry advertisements or other markings**.

q: Advertisements for which products are not allowed on playing clothing? Select all that apply.
options: Tobacco goods
Alcoholic drinks
Harmful drugs
Illegal products
Sports drinks
Banks
detail: Clothing may carry advertisements, limited in size and number, but not for **tobacco goods, alcoholic drinks, harmful drugs or illegal products**. They must not be so conspicuous or reflective as to unsight an opponent.

q: A female player's shirt is soaked and she wants to change it. What should happen?
options: She is allowed to leave the playing area to change during an authorised interval, accompanied by an official
She must change at the table
She must wait until the end of the match
She needs the opponent's permission
detail: **Female players should always be allowed to leave the field of play to change clothing**, during an authorised interval, **accompanied by an official**. It should be quick, though it may take slightly longer than the statutory interval.

q: Which of these would most referees accept a player wearing in play? Select all that apply.
options: Headgear worn for religious reasons
A headband to keep long hair out of the eyes
A reversed baseball cap
Jeans
detail: **Religious headgear** and **headbands** to keep hair out of the eyes are clearly acceptable. Most referees would **not** allow a **reversed baseball cap**, and **jeans** are not playing clothing.

q: What should the score indicators show before the players arrive, and when they arrive?
options: All blank before they arrive; game scores set to 0 when both players or pairs are in the playing area
0‑0 everywhere from the start
The previous match's final score until play begins
Blank until the first point is played
detail: Indicators are left **blank** before players arrive, as a guide to whoever controls the programme. **When both players or pairs arrive, set the game scores to 0.** Points show 0-0 only when the umpire calls it to start the game.

q: Game 3 has just ended 11-7 to A, who now leads 2 games to 1. What should the indicators show until shortly before game 4?
options: Games 1‑1, points 11‑7
Games 2‑1, points 11‑7
Games 2‑1, points blank
Games 2‑1, points 0‑0
detail: **Never show the result of a game on both the points and games indicators at the same time.** Leave the final points score up for spectators and change the games score only when the points are reset, just before the next game.

q: A manual score indicator only goes up to 20, and the game reaches 21-20 with no electronic scoreboard. What should the indicator show?
options: 11‑10: revert to 10‑10 when the flip cards run out
Leave it at 20‑20 and call the score aloud
detail: If a manual indicator only reaches about 20, **revert to 10-10**, where service alternation is expected, so 21-20 shows as 11-10. If electronic scoreboards are also used, revert to 0-0 instead (21-20 shows as 1-0) to avoid confusion.

q: To help spectators at the ends of the hall, by up to how many degrees may the operator rotate the score indicator to each side?
detail: The operator may rotate the indicator **up to 45°** to the left and/or right at suitable moments (towelling, retrieving the ball, change of service), and may raise it if it is light enough.

q: The match ends 12-10 in the fifth game, after the games were 2-2. What should the indicators show?
options: Points 12‑10 and games 2‑2
Points 12‑10 and games 3‑2
Points blank and games 3‑2
Everything blank
detail: At the end of a match, leave the indicators showing **the final points score and the previous games score**. Reset everything to blank before leaving the playing area.

q: France plays Poland in a team match. Poland wins the first individual match 3-0. What is a correct announcement?
options: “11‑6, game to Poland. Poland wins by 3 games to 0. Poland leads by 1 match to 0.”
“Poland wins. Next match.”
“3‑0 Poland, final.”
“Game, set and match Poland.”
detail: In a team match the team name may be used instead of, or as well as, the player's name. After an individual match: **“11-6, game to Poland, Poland wins by 3 games to 0; Poland leads by 1 match to 0.”**

q: For an individual event, at least how many minutes before their session should umpires report to the referee?
detail: Umpires report at least **30 minutes** before the session for individual events, and **55 minutes** for team events. Call-area duties (ball selection, racket and shirt checks, advisers) should be done at least 20 minutes before the match.

q: How should the umpire team walk into the field of play?
options: In a straight line, in step, umpire leading with the scoresheet and ball box in the left hand
Separately, each going straight to their chair
The AU leading, carrying everything
Side by side, chatting to the players
detail: The team walks in **in a straight line, in uniform step**, with **the umpire leading**, holding **the scoresheet and ball box in the left hand**. Nothing else is carried in the hands, and nothing dangles from the uniform.

q: Which items should the umpire check they have before going to the playing area? Select all that apply.
options: Net gauges (plastic and weighted)
A coin or disc for the toss
Yellow, red and white cards
Stopwatch, scoresheet and pen
A spare racket for the players
A whistle
detail: The checklist: **net gauges (plastic and weighted), a disc or coin, towel, balls, scoresheet, pen, stopwatch and coloured cards**. Officials don't supply rackets, and table tennis umpires don't use whistles.

q: What is the correct announcement sequence at the start of the first game?
options: “Keen versus Boll”, “First game”, then point to the server: “Keen to serve, love-all”
“Love-all”, then “Keen to serve”
“First game, play!”
“Keen versus Boll, best of five, play”
detail: Make sure the server has the ball and the receiver is ready, then announce the family names (**“Keen versus Boll”**), **“First game”**, and point to the server: **“Keen to serve, love-all”** (or “zero-zero”). The AU then sets the indicator to 0-0 and the timekeeper starts the clock.
